Few public questions have been debated as widely as whether employees should work from home, and opinions remain divided. Supporters of one view draw attention to the time and money that home working saves, whereas their opponents are far more concerned about the isolation of staff who work alone. Having weighed both arguments carefully, I would argue that companies should combine home working with regular office days.

Those who hold the first view place the greatest weight on these savings. The logic behind this claim is straightforward: skipping the commute means that staff start work fresher and firms need smaller offices. This pattern can be observed clearly in the case of Bangkok workers who no longer sit for hours in rush-hour traffic. That said, this argument holds only under certain conditions, and it weakens when the job needs face-to-face service, as in hospitals.

Those who take the opposite position focus instead on weaker teamwork and lower productivity, a concern that is hard to dismiss. This view rests on a clear chain of cause and effect: without casual talk in the office, small problems take longer to solve. The experience of new staff who learned their jobs over video calls during COVID-19 shows that this is not just theory. Nevertheless, this argument is often overstated, because it ignores the fact that regular online meetings can reduce much of the isolation of working alone.

Taking everything into account, I conclude that remote working cannot be judged as simply good or bad. On balance, the position I find most convincing is that a mix of home and office days works best. This seems the most reasonable answer, since it keeps the savings of home working without harming teamwork within the company.

Few recent changes have divided opinion as sharply as the shift from classroom teaching to online lessons, because its effects reach deep into the daily life of ordinary families. The strongest argument in its favour is flexible access to good teaching, whereas the most worrying cost it brings is weaker supervision and less human contact. Having weighed both sides carefully, I am convinced that the drawbacks outweigh the benefits for most teenagers.

The most persuasive reason to welcome this development is the freedom to study anywhere, which many people value highly. This advantage works in a straightforward way, by letting students replay a hard explanation at any hour. A clear illustration of this benefit can be found in the recorded lessons that many Thai schools posted on YouTube during the COVID-19 closures. Admittedly, this advantage is often smaller in practice than it first appears, since many rural families lack a stable internet connection.

This benefit, however, comes at a price: the loss of a teacher's presence, which deserves equally careful attention. This harm usually develops gradually, mainly because nobody notices when a student is confused or distracted. The real cost of this drawback was clearly visible in my own primary class during COVID-19, when many of us fell behind. Even so, this problem can be reduced, if not removed entirely, given that teachers can run short live check-ins and set daily tasks.

Taken as a whole, online schooling offers real benefits, but it also brings risks that are at least as real. Weighing one against the other, I believe that the costs are greater than the gains for secondary students. This judgement rests on one simple principle: teenagers learn best when a real teacher guides them.

Few recent changes have divided opinion as sharply as the shift from classroom teaching to online lessons at home. The strongest argument for it is flexible access to good teaching, wherever a student lives, whereas its worst cost is weaker supervision and less human contact at home. Having weighed both sides, I am convinced that the drawbacks outweigh the benefits for most teenage students.

The most persuasive reason to welcome it is the freedom to study anywhere and at any pace. This advantage works simply, by letting students pause and replay a difficult explanation at any hour until it makes sense. A clear illustration of this is the way many Thai schools posted recorded lessons on YouTube during the school closures, so students could replay them whenever they needed. Admittedly, this advantage is smaller in practice than it appears, since many rural families still lack a stable internet connection or a laptop.

This benefit, however, comes at a price: the loss of a teacher's daily presence. This harm develops because nobody in the room notices when a student is confused or distracted, so small gaps quietly grow. This drawback was clearly visible in my own primary class during COVID-19, when many of us switched off our cameras and slowly fell behind. Even so, this problem can be reduced, if not removed, given that teachers can hold short live check-ins in small groups and set daily tasks.

Taken as a whole, online schooling offers real benefits but also real risks. Weighing one against the other, I believe that the costs are greater than the gains for most secondary students. This rests on one principle: teenagers learn best when a real teacher and classmates are there to guide them.

Across many countries, online fraud against young people has grown into a serious concern that families, schools and governments can no longer ignore. This situation grows mainly out of teenagers' trust in friendly messages and cheap offers, and the most practical answer to it lies in lessons on scams at school. Having weighed the cause and the cure, I believe that schools must teach scam awareness, and banks must check risky payments.

The most important reason why this problem keeps growing is how easily young users are fooled. The cause does its damage in a fairly simple way: fake shops and hacked accounts look real, so teenagers pay without checking. A case that many young people in my city would recognise is a Facebook page selling concert tickets that never arrive. Unfortunately, the problem is made even worse by a second, separate cause: many teenagers now have banking apps, so money leaves in seconds.

To tackle this cause at its source, the most sensible response is training students to spot scams. A response like this is likely to work because students who have practised with fake messages learn to pause and check. A small example of this approach working in practice is the experience of my school, where one talk on investment scams made us careful. Even so, this measure cannot do the whole job on its own, because new tricks keep appearing, which is why banks should also delay unusual payments.

Taken together, these points show that this type of crime is not something we must accept, since its cause is known. For this reason, the best plan is that schools should lead, with banks as a safety net. This two-part plan is the most sensible one because scams need victims to hurry, and both steps slow them down.

In recent years, many societies have witnessed the shift from cash to phone payments, and this trend raises two questions that deserve careful answers. The answer to the first question lies mainly in the low cost of QR-code payment, whereas the second can best be judged by considering the safety and control digital payment gives users. Taking both answers together, I would argue that the change is mostly positive if cash remains available.

To answer the first question, the most important factor, in my view, is how cheap and simple it is to accept payment by QR code.
